cards.title: Tip
cards.body: There's no tipping anywhere: restaurants, taxis, hotels. Leaving money behind can make staff chase you to return it. Great service is just the standard.

cards.title: Stand chopsticks upright in rice
cards.body: It mirrors an offering at funerals. Rest them on the chopstick rest or across your bowl instead.

cards.title: Pass food from chopsticks to chopsticks
cards.body: This is also a funeral rite, used for the bones of the dead. Put the food on a small plate for the other person instead.

cards.title: Say thanks before and after eating
cards.body: Itadakimasu before the first bite, gochisōsama deshita to staff on the way out.
say: ごちそうさま でした
Say it as you leave a restaurant.

cards.title: Slurp your noodles
cards.body: Slurping ramen and soba is normal, and it cools the noodles. Nobody will look twice.

cards.title: Drown sushi in soy sauce
cards.body: Dip the fish side lightly, not the rice. At good sushi counters the chef may season it already. Eat it in one bite if you can.

cards.title: Pour for others, not yourself
cards.body: When drinking together, top up your companions' glasses. Someone will fill yours in return. Wait for kanpai before the first sip.

cards.title: Walk while eating
cards.body: Eating on the move is frowned on, especially in Kyoto and Nara. Eat beside the stall or the konbini where you bought it.

cards.title: Talk on the phone on trains
cards.body: Phones go on silent (manner mode), calls wait until you're off. Keep conversations quiet too.

cards.title: Queue at the floor markings
cards.body: Platforms have lines painted where the doors will open. Stand to the sides and let everyone off first.

cards.title: Stand on the correct side of escalators
cards.body: Tokyo: stand on the LEFT, walk on the right. Osaka: stand on the RIGHT. Kyoto is mixed, so follow the person in front of you.

cards.title: Wear your backpack on your front
cards.body: On crowded trains, hold your bag in front of you or put it on the overhead rack.

cards.title: Eat on local trains
cards.body: Eating on commuter trains is frowned on. On the shinkansen it's normal: a bentō box (ekiben) is part of the trip.

cards.title: Leave priority seats free
cards.body: Priority seats near the doors are for elderly, pregnant or disabled passengers. Give them up when someone needs one.

cards.title: Carry your trash
cards.body: Public bins are rare. Keep a small bag for trash and throw it out at a konbini or your hotel. Sort bins by type.

cards.title: Smoke on the street
cards.body: Many areas ban smoking outdoors, with fines. Use the marked smoking areas (喫煙所).

cards.title: Wait for the walk signal
cards.body: People wait at red lights even on empty streets, especially with kids around.

cards.title: Take your shoes off where the floor steps up
cards.body: At ryokan entrances, some restaurants, temples and fitting rooms. Point your shoes toward the door when you take them off.

cards.title: Wear slippers on tatami
cards.body: Slippers come off at the edge of the tatami. Walk on it in socks or bare feet.

cards.title: Switch to the toilet slippers
cards.body: Toilets often have their own slippers. Use them inside, then switch back. Walking out in toilet slippers is a classic tourist slip-up.

cards.title: Wear the yukata left over right
cards.body: Fold the left side over the right side of your body. Right over left is only for dressing the dead.

cards.title: Be late for ryokan dinner
cards.body: Kaiseki dinners are prepared for a set time. If you'll be late, call ahead.
say: すこし おくれます

cards.title: Wash completely before getting in
cards.body: Sit on a stool at the shower area, soap and rinse fully. The bath is for soaking, not washing.

cards.title: Put your towel in the water
cards.body: The small towel stays out of the bath. Fold it on your head or set it on the edge.

cards.title: Wear a swimsuit
cards.body: Onsen are nude and separated by gender. Look for 男 (men) and 女 (women) on the curtains. Ryokan often swap which side is which overnight.

cards.title: Ask about tattoos first
cards.body: Many onsen still ban tattoos. Small ones can sometimes be covered with a patch. A private bath (kashikiri) avoids the issue.
say: I have a tattoo. Is that OK?
タトゥーがありますが、大丈夫ですか？
タトゥーが ありますが、 だいじょうぶ ですか？
Tatū ga arimasu ga, daijōbu desu ka?

cards.title: Dry off before the changing room
cards.body: Wipe down with your small towel before stepping back into the changing area.

cards.title: Soak after drinking a lot
cards.body: Hot water plus alcohol is genuinely dangerous. Drink water and keep soaks short.

cards.title: Bow at the torii gate
cards.body: A small bow before passing through the gate shows respect. Walk along the sides of the path. The center is for the gods.

cards.title: Rinse at the water basin
cards.body: Ladle water over your left hand, then your right. Pour a little into your left palm to rinse your mouth, rinse your left hand again, then tip the ladle upright so the rest runs down the handle. Never drink straight from the ladle.

cards.title: At a shrine: bow twice, clap twice, bow once
cards.body: Toss a coin in the box, ring the bell if there is one, bow twice, clap twice, pray, then bow once more.

cards.title: Clap at a Buddhist temple
cards.body: At temples, put your hands together quietly and bow. Clapping is for Shinto shrines only.

cards.title: Take photos where it's forbidden
cards.body: Many halls ban photos inside. Look for 撮影禁止. When unsure, ask.
say: 写真を撮ってもいいですか？
しゃしんを とっても いい ですか？
Shashin o totte mo ii desu ka?

cards.title: Chase geiko or maiko for photos
cards.body: In Kyoto's Gion, private lanes ban photos and fines apply. Never block or touch them. They're working, not performing for the street.

cards.title: Bow to the deer in Nara
cards.body: Nara's deer often bow back for a cracker. They can also bite or butt when you tease them, so don't wave food around.

cards.title: Use the cash tray
cards.body: Put your money or card in the small tray on the counter. Change usually comes back in the tray too.

cards.title: Carry some cash
cards.body: Cards work in most places, but small restaurants, shrines, temples and street stalls are often cash only. 7-Eleven and Japan Post ATMs take foreign cards.

cards.title: Haggle
cards.body: Prices are fixed. Bargaining is only expected at some flea markets.

cards.title: Bring your passport for tax-free
cards.body: Tax-free needs your physical passport and ¥5,000 or more at one store in a day. Until October 31, 2026 the tax comes off at the register, and food or cosmetics come sealed: don't open them in Japan. From November 1, 2026 you pay full price, scan your passport at the airport tax-free kiosk before check-in (customs may ask to see the goods), then the store refunds the tax by the method you picked when buying. Keep receipts, and keep the goods unused until you leave.

cards.title: Give and receive with both hands
cards.body: Business cards, gifts and anything handed to you with both hands should be received with both hands and a small nod.

cards.title: Keep your voice down
cards.body: Public spaces, trains and restaurants are quieter than in the US. Lower your volume a notch or two.

cards.title: Return a small bow
cards.body: A small nod-bow is enough for a tourist. Match roughly what you receive, without overthinking it.

cards.title: Point at people
cards.body: Pointing a finger at a person is rude. Gesture with an open hand instead.

cards.title: Blow your nose at the table
cards.body: Step away to the restroom. Sniffling is considered more acceptable than blowing at the table.

cards.title: Wear a mask if you're sick
cards.body: If you have a cold, a mask in public is expected and appreciated. Konbini and drugstores sell them.

cards.title: Say sumimasen often
cards.body: Excuse me, sorry, thank you for your trouble: it covers bumping into someone, getting attention and thanking someone who helped.
